sections.content:
Mutexes are the standard tool for protecting shared data, but they carry real costs: a thread waiting on a lock is blocked and wasted, priority inversion can cause high-priority threads to stall behind low-priority ones, and a process that dies holding a lock can deadlock all waiters permanently.

**Lock-free programming** is an alternative: design data structures so that concurrent threads can always make progress without ever blocking each other. The foundation is **atomic operations** — CPU instructions guaranteed to be indivisible. A read-modify-write that completes atomically cannot be interleaved with another thread's operation, eliminating the race condition without a mutex.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Thread wants to update shared value"] --> B["Read current value"]
  B --> C["Compute new value locally"]
  C --> D["CAS: if value == expected\nthen write new value"]
  D -->|"Success"| E["Update complete"]
  D -->|"Fail - value changed"| B
sections.caption: Compare-And-Swap (CAS) loop: read, compute, attempt atomic swap. On collision, retry. No thread blocks — all make progress eventually.

sections.title: The Optimistic Checkout Analogy
sections.content:
Imagine editing a shared Google Doc offline. You download a copy (read), make your changes locally (compute), and try to sync (CAS). If nobody else changed the doc while you were offline, your changes apply immediately — success. If someone else changed it first, you see a conflict and retry with their latest version — the CAS failed and you loop.

This is **optimistic concurrency**: assume no conflict, attempt the operation, retry on collision. Compare this to a **mutex** (pessimistic concurrency): lock the door, make changes, unlock — others are blocked the entire time you're working.

Optimistic works best when conflicts are **rare** (reads heavily outnumber writes). Under high contention — everyone editing simultaneously — the retry loop becomes a spin that wastes CPU. This is the key tradeoff: lock-free is not always faster; it shines for read-heavy workloads or low-contention writes.

sections.title: Atomic Operations, CAS, and the ABA Problem
sections.content:
**Atomic operations** are CPU-level primitives that complete in a single indivisible step. Common atomic operations:
- `load` / `store` — read/write a value atomically.
- `fetch-and-add` — atomically increment and return the old value.
- `compare-and-swap (CAS)` — atomically: if `*addr == expected`, then `*addr = new`; return whether the swap succeeded.

**CAS** is the cornerstone of lock-free algorithms. Most lock-free data structures (queues, stacks, counters) reduce to loops that read, compute, and CAS, retrying on failure.

However, CAS has a famous flaw: the **ABA problem**. A CAS only checks if a value *equals* the expected value — not whether it *was stable* throughout the interval. Suppose thread T1 reads `A`, gets preempted, thread T2 changes the value `A → B → A`, and T1's CAS succeeds because the value is `A` again — even though the underlying structure has changed. Solutions include:
- **Tagged pointers / version stamps**: pair the value with a monotonically increasing counter. `CAS(addr, {A, v1}, {new, v2})` fails if the version changed, even if the value reverted.
- **Hazard pointers / epoch-based reclamation**: for pointer-based structures, defer freeing memory until no thread holds a reference.

**Lock-free vs wait-free:**
- **Lock-free**: at least one thread makes progress in a finite number of steps. Other threads may retry indefinitely under adversarial scheduling, but the *system* as a whole does not stall.
- **Wait-free**: every individual thread completes its operation in a bounded number of steps, regardless of other threads. Stronger guarantee, much harder to implement (e.g., Fetch-And-Add for counters is naturally wait-free).

**Memory barriers / fences** are equally critical. Modern CPUs and compilers reorder instructions for performance. Without barriers, a thread might observe a stale cached value even after another thread has written a new one. `Atomics.store` / `Atomics.load` in JavaScript and `std::atomic` in C++ include appropriate barriers by default.

sections.caption: ABA problem: T1's CAS succeeds because the value returned to A, but the intermediate B→A change may have invalidated structural invariants.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: `Atomics.add` is a single indivisible CPU instruction — no two threads can interleave their read-modify-write. The atomic counter will always equal `4 × ITERATIONS`. The racy counter (non-atomic increment) loses updates when threads read the same value before either writes back, demonstrating the data race that lock-free programming eliminates.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Lock-free is not always faster.** Under low contention, atomic operations beat mutexes significantly. Under high contention, CAS retry loops become spin-waste — threads thrash and burn CPU without progress. Always benchmark your actual contention level. For most application-level code, a well-tuned mutex or a message-passing actor is simpler and nearly as fast. Reserve lock-free structures for proven bottlenecks: counters, ring buffers, and concurrent queues in hot paths.

items: **Atomic operations** are indivisible CPU instructions — no thread can observe a partial execution, eliminating the read-modify-write race condition without locks.
**Compare-And-Swap (CAS)** is the fundamental primitive: atomically write a new value only if the current value equals an expected one; retry in a loop on failure.
The **ABA problem** occurs when a value changes A→B→A between a CAS read and write; the swap succeeds incorrectly. Fix with version stamps or tagged pointers.
**Lock-free** guarantees system-wide progress (at least one thread advances); **wait-free** guarantees per-thread bounded progress — a strictly stronger guarantee.
**Memory barriers** prevent compiler and CPU reordering from exposing stale cached values; JavaScript's `Atomics` API includes implicit barriers on every operation.

quiz.question: What makes an operation 'atomic' in the context of concurrent programming?
options: It executes faster than non-atomic operations
It completes as a single indivisible step — no other thread can observe a partial execution
It uses a mutex internally
It runs on a dedicated CPU core
quiz.explanation: An atomic operation appears instantaneous to all other threads — they either see the state before or after the operation, never a halfway state. This eliminates the window for race conditions without requiring a lock.

quiz.question: In a CAS (Compare-And-Swap) operation, when does the swap FAIL?
options: When the new value equals the expected value
When the memory address is not cache-aligned
When the current value of the target differs from the expected value
When more than two threads attempt the CAS simultaneously
quiz.explanation: CAS atomically checks if `*addr == expected`. If another thread has modified `*addr` since the reading thread last checked, the values differ and the CAS returns without writing. The calling thread typically retries by re-reading the current value.

quiz.question: What is the ABA problem?
options: A deadlock caused by three threads acquiring locks in the wrong order
A CAS succeeding incorrectly because a value changed A→B→A, making the swap appear safe when the underlying structure has changed
An algorithm that requires alternating read and write operations
A memory leak caused by atomic operations not releasing memory
quiz.explanation: ABA: Thread T1 reads A, gets preempted. Thread T2 changes A→B→A. T1's CAS succeeds because the value is A again, but the intermediate changes may have invalidated invariants (e.g., freed and reallocated memory at the same address).

quiz.question: What is the difference between lock-free and wait-free progress guarantees?
options: Lock-free means no locks; wait-free means threads wait for each other
Lock-free guarantees system-wide progress (at least one thread advances); wait-free guarantees every individual thread completes in bounded steps
They are identical guarantees with different names
Wait-free is weaker than lock-free because threads may wait indefinitely
quiz.explanation: Lock-free ensures the system always makes progress — at least one thread finishes. Wait-free is stronger: every thread finishes within a bounded number of steps regardless of what other threads do. `Atomics.add` is wait-free; a CAS retry loop is lock-free but not wait-free.

quiz.question: Which JavaScript API provides atomic operations on a `SharedArrayBuffer`?
options: Mutex
SharedLock
Atomics
Interlocked
quiz.explanation: JavaScript's `Atomics` object provides atomic read, write, add, and CAS operations on typed arrays backed by a `SharedArrayBuffer`. It also provides `Atomics.wait` and `Atomics.notify` for blocking/signaling between workers.

quiz.question: Why do modern CPUs and compilers sometimes reorder memory operations, and how does this affect concurrent code?
options: Reordering is always safe — CPUs guarantee sequential consistency
Reordering optimizes single-threaded performance but can cause other threads to observe stale or out-of-order values without memory barriers
Reordering only affects single-threaded programs
CPUs never reorder writes, only reads
quiz.explanation: Out-of-order execution and store buffering optimize performance for single threads. In concurrent code, another thread may observe a stale cached value or see writes in a different order than they occurred. Memory barriers / fences enforce ordering constraints across threads.

quiz.question: What is the standard fix for the ABA problem in pointer-based lock-free data structures?
options: Use a global mutex around all CAS operations
Pair each pointer with a monotonically increasing version stamp and include both in the CAS
Avoid all pointer-based structures and use arrays only
Require threads to register before performing CAS
quiz.explanation: A version stamp (or tag) increases on every write. A CAS checks both the pointer and the version, so A→B→A results in version v1→v2→v3. T1's CAS expects version v1 but finds v3, detecting the ABA cycle even though the pointer reverted.

quiz.question: Under high contention, a CAS-based lock-free counter performs WORSE than a mutex-protected counter because:
options: CAS cannot handle more than two threads
Multiple threads spin in retry loops, wasting CPU cycles without making net progress
Mutexes use hardware acceleration unavailable to CAS
Atomics are not supported by all CPUs
quiz.explanation: Under high contention, many threads attempt CAS simultaneously. Most fail and retry — burning CPU in a tight spin loop. A mutex-blocked thread is descheduled and wastes no CPU. For hot write paths, mutex + sleep or partitioned counters (one per core, summed when needed) often outperform a single atomic.

quiz.question: `Atomics.add(view, 0, 1)` is considered wait-free because:
options: It uses a CAS retry loop internally
It acquires a lock for exactly one instruction
It completes in a single hardware instruction with no retry — every caller succeeds immediately
It is limited to one thread at a time
quiz.explanation: Fetch-and-Add is a single atomic machine instruction on x86 (`LOCK XADD`) and ARM. Every thread that calls it completes immediately — there is no retry loop and no thread can be delayed by another. This is the definition of wait-free.

quiz.question: When is a lock-free approach most appropriate over a mutex?
options: When critical sections are long and complex
When contention is high and many threads compete for the same data
For read-heavy workloads or short, low-contention writes in performance-critical paths
Whenever you need correctness — lock-free is always safer
quiz.explanation: Lock-free shines for read-heavy access (reads can proceed without any blocking) or infrequent writes where CAS rarely retries. Under high write contention, retrying CAS loops waste CPU. Always profile first: mutexes with low contention can be faster than any lock-free structure.
